title: Robust sample average approximation
contribution: Proposes Robust SAA, distributionally robust optimization over the confidence region of a goodness-of-fit test, which keeps SAA's tractability (LP/SOCP reformulations, polynomial-time results) and asymptotic convergence and adds a finite-sample guarantee; characterizes the finite-sample and asymptotic behaviour of any data-driven DRO by the significance and (uniform) consistency of the test it implies, introduces an LCX-based multivariate test and a 'price of data', and shows on synthetic newsvendor and portfolio problems that the method is valid, convergent and more stable than SAA, two-sample SAA and Delage-Ye (read as arXiv v3).
problem_entry: RO+DA (AP testbeds): SAA is credited with tractability and almost-sure convergence but has no finite-sample guarantee and is unstable at moderate N; hold-out (two-sample) SAA sacrifices half the data and its bound can fail; data-driven DRO (Delage-Ye, Calafiore-El Ghaoui) has a finite-sample guarantee but no convergence; goal: keep SAA's virtues and add a guarantee, in the historical-data setting with one fixed sample (pp. 1-5).
key_idea: Use as uncertainty set the confidence region of a GoF test fixed before seeing the data; by the duality of tests and confidence regions every data-driven set is some test, significance gives the finite-sample guarantee (Prop. 1) and a new property, uniform consistency, characterizes convergence (Thm. 2, iff); intersect with a moment test when support is unbounded (Prop. 2 fix); a new LCX test covers joint distributions (pp. 7-15).
assumptions: min E_F[c(x;xi)] with IID data from unknown F and one fixed sample; equicontinuity in x, X bounded or uniformly coercive, bounded support or a dominating phi (Assumptions 1-3); simple hypotheses only; for tractability the cost is a max of K pieces convex in x (and concave in xi for LCX), size 2^K - 1; thresholds distribution-free, proven (Thm. 16) or bootstrapped (approximate); synthetic newsvendor demands and a 10-asset factor model with Pareto tails, no real data (pp. 5-6, 13, 16, 19-22, 24, 28).
proof_devices: Two-line finite-sample guarantee: F in the region implies the robust value bounds the true cost, so the probability is at least 1 - alpha (Prop. 1, p. 8)

Iff characterization: uniformly consistent test <=> convergence of objectives, optimal values and solutions under Assumptions 1-3 (Thm. 2, p. 13); only-if via portmanteau lemma and uniform integrability (Props. 8-9, pp. 36-37); if via four costs ||x||(2 +/- cos x'xi), ||x||(2 +/- sin x'xi) with Levy continuity and Cramer-Wold (pp. 37-38)
Constructed counterexample test (dyadic-interval acceptance plus re-levelled KS) that is consistent but not uniformly consistent (Prop. 4, pp. 35-36)

Uniform consistency of chi2/G via Cauchy-Schwarz and Pinsker bounds on total variation; KS/Kuiper via the Levy metric; CvM/AD/Watson via counting (Thms. 4-5, pp. 38-39); LCX via integrated hinge functions and Cramer-Wold (Thm. 7, p. 40); c-consistency of marginals for separable costs and of moment sets for quadratic costs (Props. 5-6, pp. 14-15)
Fenchel duality of phi-divergences giving SOCP (chi2) and exponential-cone (G) counterparts (Thm. 8, pp. 16, 40-41)

Univariate test constraints written as canonical cones in F0(xi_(i)) and semi-infinite conic duality with the empirical distribution as generalized Slater point (Thms. 10-12, pp. 17-18 fn. 4); worst case supported on at most N+1 points (p. 19)
Conjugate-based LP with upper and lower bounds for the LCX set, exact under a sub-quadratic condition (Thm. 14, pp. 21-22, 43-45)
Polynomial-time results via weak separation = weak optimization (Grotschel-Lovasz-Schrijver) (Thms. 9, 13, 15; pp. 16, 19, 22, 42, 45)
Closed-form KS newsvendor certified by a primal-dual feasible pair with equal objectives (Prop. 7, pp. 19, 42-43)
Exact LCX threshold from a VC-dimension (d+1) relative-deviation bound; bootstrap threshold needs a nonconvex sup solved by MILP or discretization (Thm. 16 and section 10.3, pp. 34-35)
Price of data estimated by resampling one extra point, plus a closed-form KS-newsvendor approximation (eqs. 43-45, p. 23)
experiments: Gurobi 5.5 (LP/SOCP) and IPOPT 3.11 (AD test); no machine or solve times anywhere; alpha = 20% for all methods; replications per N set so the mean's standard error is at most 0.1 SD, plots of means with 20th-80th percentile bars. Newsvendor (b = 19, h = 1, N = 10 to 10^8): SAA below the full-information optimum 65% of the time at N = 100, two-sample SAA about twice SAA's variance, Delage-Ye converging to Scarf's bound, Robust SAA valid, convergent and less variable; five GoF tests comparable, KS recommended as simplest; multi-item newsvendor converges as c-consistency predicts. Portfolio (10 assets, CVaR 10%, LCX test, bootstrapped Delage-Ye thresholds for fairness): two-sample SAA's guarantee holds only about 50-60% of the time against 80%, Robust SAA's holds in all samples with the best average out-of-sample suboptimality and lowest decision variance. Synthetic data only; failures reported only for competitors (pp. 24-30).
positioning: Unifies SAA (Shapiro; Kleywegt-Shapiro-Homem-de-Mello; Mak-Morton-Wood for two-sample SAA), DRO (Scarf 1958; moment sets incl. Bertsimas-Popescu; Wiesemann-Kuhn-Sim) and GoF testing; criticizes data-driven DRO [13, 15] for missing asymptotics and re-derives them as two-moment tests; shows Wang-Glynn-Ye's unbounded KS set gives an infinite bound; positions the trio's own data-driven RO [7] as a finite-sample cousin; credits and extends phi-divergence work; rivals restated and even improved (bootstrapped Delage-Ye) rather than attacked; no Wasserstein-ball DRO paper among the 56 references (pp. 2-5, 7-8, 10, 15, 25, 28, 30-32).
writing: Grants the incumbent two virtues before naming two faults; six numbered contributions incl. the price of data; boxed three-step recipe; 'this is key' marks the property rivals lack; 'In our opinion' for judgements; findings listed as bullets before the experiments; one summary table of convergence status with tightness marks and a '?' for the open case; explicit open question with a conjecture; all proofs but one in the appendix; hedged generalization of test rankings (pp. 2-3, 7, 12-13, 15, 23-24, 27-28).
limits_future: LCX uniform consistency for unbounded support left open (conjectured true); marginals test weak in high dimension; reformulation size 2^K; exponential cone numerically challenging; bootstrap thresholds only approximate; composite hypotheses excluded; unstated: synthetic data only and no run times; the conclusion gives no further agenda (pp. 6, 11, 13, 15-16, 22, 30).

method_links.note: Data-driven DRO reduced to LP/SOCP for off-the-shelf solvers (incl. two-stage linear recourse), dual reading (worst case on at most N+1 points) and printed boundary (exponential cone, 2^K growth, open LCX case); the test is chosen for the simplest optimization problem. Tractability here means solver class (off-the-shelf LP/SOCP) with no timings, between the 2004 complexity sense and the 2019 solve-time sense.

One data-set knob (significance alpha, via a statistical test) with a solution-independent guarantee P(bound >= true cost) >= 1 - alpha, plus a new 'price of data'; but alpha is fixed at 20% in all experiments and no price curve over alpha is published.

Duel against the incumbent SAA, its hold-out variant and Delage-Ye (upgraded to bootstrapped thresholds for fairness) on synthetic data with a known full-information optimum; convex problems, so no MIO, warm start, certificate or time limit, and no run times reported.
Decisions scored by true out-of-sample cost, empirical coverage of each bound and variance of the recommended decisions rather than estimation accuracy; but no owner, current rule or real data.
Two of his students (Gupta, Kallus, in SKILL.md's RO and DA lineages) on one paper; a sibling paper by the same trio on data-driven uncertainty sets cited as [7].

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: exact dictionary between a statistical procedure and a robust model, with its boundary
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Significance <-> finite-sample guarantee and uniform consistency <-> convergence (an iff, with tightness marks); rivals' data-driven sets re-read as two-moment tests; the same move recurs in S085 (regularization <-> robustification) and S104 (regularized SVM = feature-robust SVM); related to Heuristic 1

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: upgrade the rival with the new lens before the duel
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Once Delage-Ye's set is read as a hypothesis test, its thresholds are bootstrapped, tightening its bound, and the improved version is the opponent

transferable: Build the uncertainty set as the confidence region of a GoF test at level alpha chosen before seeing the data; the finite-sample guarantee follows in two lines (Prop. 1, p. 8).

Compare competing data-driven sets by converting each into the test it implies and checking (c-)consistency for your cost: separable costs need only marginal tests, costs quadratic in xi only moment tests (pp. 7, 13-15).
If unbounded support makes the robust bound infinite (Prop. 2), intersect the region with a test on E[phi(xi)] for a phi dominating the cost and split the level by the union bound (p. 10).
Dualize the sup over distributions by conic duality with the empirical distribution as generalized Slater point; the worst case then has at most N+1 support points (pp. 18-19).
Estimate the value of one more observation by resampling: PoD ~ z(data) minus the average of z(data plus a copy of xi_i) (eq. 44, p. 23).

Protocol: replications per N so the standard error is at most 0.1 SD; means with 20th-80th percentile bars; report each bound's empirical coverage and the variance of decisions, not only of objectives (pp. 24-29).
coauthors: Vishal Gupta (Marshall School of Business, USC), Nathan Kallus (ORIE and Cornell Tech, Cornell); NSF Graduate Research Fellowship 1122374

quotes.text: Unlike other data-driven DRO proposals, however – and this is key – we prove that Robust SAA also satisfies an asymptotic convergence property similar to SAA.
For practical purposes, if the convergence rates are comparable as they are here, we recommend to choose the test that yields the simplest optimization problem, which in this case is the KS test.

title: Characterization of the equivalence of robustification and regularization in linear and matrix regression
contribution: Characterizes exactly when adversarial robustification of a regression problem equals penalized regularization: a general equivalence for induced seminorm uncertainty sets, an induced-regularizer upper bound for any compact set, tight two-sided bounds via a norm-discrepancy function with iff conditions (equivalence for l_p loss only when p is 1, q or infinity), a claim that non-equivalent problems can have disjoint solution paths, and an extension to matrix completion (nuclear norm as robustification) and PCA (robust PCA arises only with an F1 loss); read as arXiv v2.
problem_entry: RO+ML: known instances in which a regularized regression equals a robustified one (El Ghaoui-Lebret, Xu-Caramanis-Mannor, Ben-Tal et al.) and the rise of adversarial ML prompt the question of exactly when the two coincide and whether the link extends to matrix problems; stated as min-max over U versus loss plus penalty (pp. 1-2, 4-5, 7).
key_idea: For any compact U the robust loss is bounded above by g(z) + h(beta) with induced regularizer h(beta) = max g(Delta beta), tight at z = 0; equivalence means tightness for every z, which holds for induced sets (Thm. 1) and fails otherwise by a computable discrepancy delta_m (Thm. 4); matrix analogues via linear perturbation maps; convex surrogates (l1, nuclear norm) arise from l0- and rank-induced sets (pp. 7-12, 17-20).
assumptions: Convex loss g (norm or seminorm), penalized-form regularization only, additive uncertainty in X only (uncertainty in y folded into a new loss), norm-ball sets of fixed radius lambda > 0 (induced, Frobenius, spectral), m >= 2 for strictness, l2 rather than squared l2 loss for ridge/Lasso; linear perturbation maps for matrices; no data (pp. 3-6, 8, 12, 17).
proof_devices: Upper bound by the triangle inequality and a matching rank-one worst case Delta = (lambda/g(z)) z v' with v the dual-norm maximizer of beta; separate case g(z) = 0 (Thm. 1, pp. 7-8)
Two set inclusions show the l0-induced set equals the l1-induced set (Prop. 1, pp. 9-10)
Seminorm axioms for the induced regularizer h(beta) = max over U of g(Delta beta) (Prop. 2, pp. 10-11)

Holder chain plus rank-one attainer for the upper bound, sign alignment for equality at p in {1, infinity}, Minkowski equality condition and finiteness of argmax delta_m for strictness, rank-one Delta for the lower bound (Thm. 4, Appendix A pp. 27-28)
Tightness of the lower bound by scaling z to alpha z, a directional-derivative limit and an epsilon-net of the q-sphere (Appendix A, pp. 28-30)
Reduction max over U of ||z + Delta beta|| = max over ||u|| <= lambda||beta|| of ||z + u|| ('Theorem 4 in disguise', Props. 3-4, pp. 14-15)

Three-point example for disjoint robust and regularized paths (Thm. 5, Appendix B p. 31); my recomputation of the example as printed gives robust minimizer (3 - lambda)/(5 + lambda^2), which lies on the regularization path [0, 3/5), so it does not show disjointness; beta* = 3/5 for all lambda holds only with radius lambda (uncertainty in y)
experiments: n/a: no computations, data or solvers; the only numbers are the three-point example of Appendix B (p. 31), whose printed conclusion my grid recomputation does not reproduce.
positioning: Credits the equivalence line (El Ghaoui-Lebret, Xu-Caramanis-Mannor, Caramanis-Mannor-Xu, Ben-Tal-El Ghaoui-Nemirovski) and labels Corollary 1 and Theorems 2-3 as theirs; differs by aim (characterization, not tractability or the Lasso's implications); claims no connection to robust statistics; casts total least squares as the optimistic counterpart of the adversarial min-max; matrix side builds on Candes-Recht, Recht-Fazel-Parrilo, Candes-Li-Ma-Wright; adversarial deep learning only as motivation (pp. 2, 5-10, 16-17, 19).
writing: Two numbered contributions with one strong phrase ('We break new ground'); definition-theorem-proof, each result followed by a one-paragraph reading (elastic net as 'feature-wise' and 'global' perturbations; 'Theorem 4 in disguise'); two summary tables (loss x set x penalty x iff condition) carry the message; borrowed results credited explicitly; four-sentence conclusion with no future directions (pp. 2, 7-10, 14-15, 22-23).
limits_future: Theory only (no algorithm, software or application); penalized form only; additive uncertainty in X only; other uncertainty sets not examined in depth; most matrix proofs omitted and Prop. 8 stated without proof; the motivating use (data-driven sets designing regularizers) not attempted; Appendix B example fails as printed and carries typos (my recomputation); no future work stated (pp. 2, 4-6, 17-23, 31).

method_links.note: A procedure owned by statistics (penalized regression) is rewritten as a min-max problem, structure is read off dual norms (rank-one worst case) and the boundary is printed as iff tables; but the boundary is of equivalence, not of solver class or solve time, and nothing is solved.

The radius lambda is an interpretable knob equal to the regularization weight under equivalence, and the elastic net's two weights control two perturbation types; outside equivalence the link is lost and paths may be disjoint; no curve, no data.
Written with a doctoral student (Copenhaver, ORC, NDSEG fellow); its result is consumed by the group's next robust-ML paper (S104) to justify dropping the SVM regularizer.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: exact dictionary between a statistical procedure and a robust model, with its boundary
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Regularization <-> robustification with iff conditions and two-sided bounds where it fails (Tables 2-3); full-text evidence for Heuristic 1 with a nuance: Lasso-as-robustification is credited to Xu-Caramanis-Mannor, the paper's own contribution is where the reading breaks; also in S039 and S104

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: derive the convex surrogate from an uncertainty set induced by the nonconvex penalty
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: l1 arises from an l0-induced uncertainty set and the nuclear norm from a rank-induced set, without a convex-envelope argument

transferable: To prove that a robust problem equals a regularized one: bound above with the triangle inequality, then exhibit a rank-one worst case built from the dual-norm maximizer of beta (pp. 7-8).
Use h(beta) = max over U of g(Delta beta) as the canonical induced regularizer of any compact uncertainty set; equivalence holds iff this upper bound is tight for every residual (Prop. 2, pp. 10-11).
Quantify a failed equivalence with norm-discrepancy constants and prove them tight by a scaling limit plus an epsilon-net (pp. 11-12, 28-30).
Close a characterization paper with one table: loss x uncertainty set x induced penalty x iff condition (Tables 2-3, pp. 15, 22).
Check a small counterexample numerically before printing it; Appendix B's example fails as printed (p. 31; my recomputation).
coauthors: Martin S. Copenhaver (Operations Research Center, MIT; NDSEG fellowship)

quotes.text: This proposition implies that ℓ1 arises from the robustification setting without directly appealing to standard convexity arguments for why ℓ1 should be used to replace ℓ0
As a result, when robustification and regularization do not coincide, they can induce structurally distinct solutions.

title: Robust classification
contribution: Derives feature-robust, label-robust and robust-in-both counterparts of SVM, logistic regression and optimal classification trees (norm-ball feature sets; a budget Gamma of flipped labels dualized through an integral polytope), and shows on synthetic data (2,000 repetitions) and 75 UCI data sets that robustness usually helps against nominal models, with the largest gains (5.3% SVM, 4.0% logistic regression, 1.3% trees vs CART) above a hand-set rule on dimension and nominal accuracy; gains over regularized models are smaller (0.5% and 1.9% above the line), and the label-robust SVM is formulated as an MIO although an exact LP exists (my derivation).
problem_entry: ML+RO+IO: training data carry feature errors (measurement, imputation) and label errors (survey dishonesty, subjective clinical labels, labelling staff), handled so far mainly by regularization; prior robust classifiers are feature-only, theoretical, little tested, and robust trees do not exist; goal: robust counterparts for the three most-used classifiers, tested against nominal and regularized versions (pp. 2-5).
key_idea: One recipe: training as an optimization problem (trees via the OCT MIO), an uncertainty set, a dualized inner worst case; features via the dual-norm lemma (margin shift, logit-exponent penalty, split margin rho), labels via a binary flip budget whose integral polytope makes LP duality exact; nominal SVM stripped of its regularizer to avoid double counting; knobs rho and Gamma validated with zero nested (pp. 6-19).
assumptions: Binary labels; per-point l_q feature balls of radius rho (Cartesian product, chosen for one knob and a geometric reading), q = infinity in experiments; at most Gamma flipped labels; univariate big-M OCT trees with minbucket; synthetic R2 clusters with 10 random-label outliers and an outlier-free test set; 75 UCI data sets as one-vs-rest problems, n up to 245,057 and p up to 857 (pp. 5-10, 13, 19-21).
proof_devices: Dual-norm lemma max over ||x||_q <= rho of a'x = rho ||a||_q* applied to SVM margins, logistic exponents and tree splits (eq. 7 and Thms. 1-3, pp. 9-12)
Monotonicity of the log-likelihood in the margin reduces the inner minimum to the dual-norm problem; first-order Taylor link between feature-robust and regularized logistic regression (pp. 11-12)
Univariate splits have ||a_j||_q* = 1, so feature robustness is a margin rho around each threshold and stays a linear MIO for any q (Thm. 3, p. 12)

Binary flip makes each loss term affine in the flip; integral budget polytope makes the LP relaxation exact; strong duality yields the label-robust counterparts (Thms. 4-6, pp. 13-17); composition for robust-in-both (Thms. 7-9, Appendix B pp. 32-33)
Geometric reading of label-robust trees: each leaf needs a strict majority with margin 2Gamma (p. 17)
Appendix A: regularized SVM is exactly a feature-robust hinge loss under an aggregate set (Fertis 2009) (pp. 31-32)

My recomputation: substituting s_i = r_i + xi_i turns Thm. 4's MIO into the LP min Gamma q + sum s_i, s_i >= max(1 - m_i, 0), q + s_i >= max(1 + m_i, 0), q >= 0; equal optimal values to scenario-enumeration LP and the paper's MIO (19) on six small random instances (scipy HiGHS); and in Thm. 5 log((1+e^-m)/(1+e^m)) = -m, so label-robust logistic regression has linear constraints (pp. 13-15)
experiments: Julia/JuMP, Gurobi (version not given), IPOPT, RPART 4.1-9. Synthetic: 2,000 repetitions, out-of-sample error and distance to the true hyperplane; robust-in-both best (SVM 2.363% vs nominal 2.571% and regularized 2.643%; 90th percentile 3.325% vs 3.941%), but feature-robust logistic regression is slightly worse than regularized at three percentiles despite 'across the board'. Real: 75 UCI sets, 60/20/20 split, 5 splits; wins/losses/ties vs nominal e.g. SVM-both 39/20/16, LR-both 40/20/15, CART-both 33/24/18 (only two rows exceed half of all 75 sets); hand-set rule log10(p) >= 0.05a - 2.5 chosen and judged on the same 75 sets: above it +5.3/+4.0/+1.3% (and +1.4% vs nominal OCT), below about zero; vs nominal OCT overall 24 wins, 28 losses; vs regularized above the line +0.5% (SVM) and +1.9% (LR), overall SVM 26 wins vs 35 losses, while contribution 4 states 2.1% and 1.2%. Timing on one thread of a Xeon E5-2687W with a 1-hour limit and time-to-best-solution: label robustness said to slow by 1-2 orders, but at least 23 of 53 robust cells take 10x or more and five more than 1,000x; accuracy runs stopped at an unstated time limit; no certificates or gaps (pp. 19-31).
positioning: Builds on Xu-Caramanis-Mannor (robustness behind SVM regularization) and Bertsimas-Copenhaver (S085, the double-counting argument); credits feature-robust SVM/LR to Xu et al., Fertis, El Ghaoui et al., Harrington et al.; sets apart Trafalis-Gilbert (double counting), heuristic label-noise SVMs and robust statistics (passive evaluation vs active model construction); kernel methods out of scope; own lines OCT, best subset, least quantile and algorithmic regression; borrows NETLIB evidence from Ben-Tal-Nemirovski and the price-of-robustness title from Bertsimas-Sim (pp. 2-5, 8-11, 30).
writing: Abstract moves from data inaccuracies to 'does not materially change the complexity' to headline gains limited to 'high-dimensional and difficult' problems; 'principled' as the distinguishing adjective; each theorem closes on 'practically solvable'; four numbered contributions; hedged explanations of odd results; section titled after the 2004 paper; two headline-body divergences (complexity claim vs Tables 9-10; contribution 4's percentages vs Table 8) (pp. 2-4, 14, 18-19, 24, 27-30).
limits_future: Stated: kernel methods out of scope; norm-ball sets only; robust-in-both validation may miss the best combination; MIO time limits may cap accuracy, longer limits could improve it; one infeasible instance. Unstated: decision rule fitted and judged on the same 75 data sets; no certificates or gaps; time limit of the accuracy runs; a class-keeping LP for the label-robust SVM. No further agenda (pp. 4, 10, 24, 30-31).

method_links.note: Feature robustness keeps every class and label robustness keeps trees MIO and logistic regression convex, but the label-robust SVM leaves its class (LP to MIO) at measured costs of up to about three orders of magnitude, while the abstract says complexity is not materially changed; a verified exact LP reformulation shows a class-keeping device existed, so Method 1's stop rule (change the device, not the solver) applies (Tension T4).

Bertsimas-Sim's budget Gamma reused as a cardinality bound on flipped labels and a section titled 'The Price of Robustness'; knobs set from data by validation with the nominal at zero, as the method's correction asks; but no price curve over rho or Gamma, the price being read as accuracy and solve time.

Incumbents as opponents (nominal, l1-regularized, RPART CART, nominal OCT) on synthetic truth (2,000 repetitions) and 75 UCI data sets with five splits; trees warm-started (exploration depth around the warm start); step 6 (say where the method wins) turned into an explicit rule.
The certificate step is dropped on purpose: reported times are times to the best solution, not to proof, and the accuracy runs stop at an unstated 'smaller time limit'; evidence for Tension T1.
The why-now argument is asserted without a number: MIO successes attributed to dramatic hardware and software gains over the past 30 years.
A cohort of three students (Dunn, Pawlowski, Zhuo) on one paper, extending the OCT programme into robust optimization; published in IJOO's first issue.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: a when-to-use rule for practitioners, fitted on the benchmark
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: A hand-set line log10(p) >= 0.05a - 2.5 on dimension and nominal in-sample accuracy, said to predict 'with high accuracy' when robustness helps, chosen and judged on the same 75 data sets; related to Method 4 step 6

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: nest the nominal model at knob zero in validation
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: rho = Gamma = 0 lies in every validation grid, so a robust model is adopted only when it validates better

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: exact dictionary between a statistical procedure and a robust model, with its boundary
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Regularized SVM is a feature-robust hinge loss, so the regularizer is stripped before robustness is added (double counting); label robustness has no regularization analogue; also in S039 and S085

transferable: Model label noise as a budget Gamma of flips: each loss term is affine in the binary flip, the budget polytope is integral, so dualize its LP relaxation; for a hinge loss substitute s_i = r_i + xi_i to keep the counterpart an LP (pp. 13-17; LP form is my derivation, checked numerically).
Put the nominal model inside the validation grid (rho = Gamma = 0) so the robust variant is chosen only when it validates better (pp. 9, 13, 17).
Strip the nominal model's built-in robustness (its regularizer) before adding explicit robustness, then compare against both the nominal and the regularized model (pp. 3, 10, 27).

Synthetic recovery test: plant a known separating hyperplane, contaminate the training data, report out-of-sample error, distance to the true hyperplane and error percentiles over 2,000 repetitions (pp. 19-20).
Timing protocol: one thread, stated machine, one-hour limit, and a flag on every time that is not a proven optimum (pp. 29-30).
Report wins/losses/ties per data set beside average gains (Tables 4-6, 8; pp. 24-29); critic-informed, not his practice: hold out data sets when fitting a when-to-use rule.
coauthors: Jack Dunn, Colin Pawlowski, Ying Daisy Zhuo (Sloan School and Operations Research Center, MIT); NSF Graduate Research Fellowship 1122374

quotes.text: We show that adding robustness does not materially change the complexity of the problem and that all robust counterparts can be solved in practical computational times.

In a real-world application of these methods, the time taken to find the solution is the more important measure than the time taken to prove the solution optimal; therefore, time to finding solution is used.
